newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN appeals for cash to monitor Rwanda refugees.
newsitem.headline: UN appeals for cash to monitor Rwanda refugees.

text.p: The cash-strapped United Nations human rights body made an urgent appeal on Monday to Western donors to cough up money to boost the number of field observers to encourage Rwandan Hutu refugees to come home.

Jose Ayala-Lasso, the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, said at least 200 observers were needed in Rwanda, nearly double the present figure, and another 35 in neighbouring Burundi where there are only a handful of them.

A U.N. statement issued in Geneva said Ayala-Lasso urged his staff in Rwanda and Burundi to step up the monitoring of Hutu returnees fleeing conflict between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi fighters in eastern Zaire.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR says only 1,700 Rwandan Hutus have braved the journey home since fighting broke out in eastern Zaire two weeks ago while some 11,000 Burundian Hutus have returned to Burundi.

East Zaire is home to a million Rwandan Hutus who fled after 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis and fear revenge at the hands of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. Since fighting broke out, half a million are now on the move and their camps have been emptied.
Rwanda says it wants the refugees home but diplomats say its Tutsi-dominated government has failed to go the extra mile.

Hundreds of Hutus have been killed by Tutsi soldiers in reprisals. More than 80,000 Hutu genocide suspects are crammed into overcrowded jails with no files and first trials have been repeatedly delayed.

Ayala-Lasso said more human rights observers were needed to ensure that refugee returnees were not arrested arbitrarily or treated violently and that their homes were not occupied in Rwanda and Burundi, according to the statement.

In Burundi, several hundred people were killed when they recently tried to return to villages near Gatumba transit point, it said. Human rights observers and aid officials were blocked from entering the transit area near Zaire's border, it added.
The ethnic war raging between Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels means the U.N. monitors in Burundi can rarely travel to the terrain and are often blocked by soldiers.

The UNHCR has appealed to Rwandan Hutus to flee eastern Zaire's spreading conflict and return to Rwanda, Africa's most crowded country where a centuries-old rivalry over farmland has been at the root of the animosity between Hutus and Tutsis.

Border regions in Rwanda are ill-prepared for an influx of refugees. More than 800,000 Tutsis who fled abroad during earlier bouts of ethnic conflict have returned home since Tutsis swept to power in 1994. The new Tutsi arrivals have settled in abandoned homes of Hutu refugees who fled to Zaire.
Some Tutsis, trying to quash property claims of returning Hutus, are said to have falsely accused them of taking part in the genocide.
